excerpt: Maximum medical improvement means your condition has stabilized, not that you are healed. Why MMI is the turning point in an injury claim.
keyTakeaways: Maximum medical improvement (MMI) is when your condition stabilizes — not when you are fully healed. In Georgia, MMI is when your impairment rating is assigned; PPD (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-263) is paid once TTD or TPD ends, and MMI alone does not end TTD; catastrophic injuries are not subject to the 400-week caps (O.C.G.A. §§ 34-9-261, 34-9-200.1). In South Carolina, MMI triggers PPD within the 500-week cap (S.C. Code § 42-9-10, § 42-9-30). Medical benefits continue after MMI in both states, subject to Georgia's 400-week limit for non-catastrophic injuries. Do not settle a PI case before reaching MMI — and challenge premature determinations.

faqs.question: What is maximum medical improvement (MMI)?
faqs.answer: MMI is the point when your treating physician determines that your condition has stabilized and is unlikely to improve significantly with further treatment. It does not mean you are fully healed — it means you have recovered as much as you are going to. Your doctor assigns an impairment rating at MMI that quantifies any permanent loss of function.

faqs.question: Who determines when I have reached MMI?
faqs.answer: Your treating physician makes the MMI determination. However, the workers' comp insurer or the opposing party's insurance company may request an Independent Medical Examination (IME) if they disagree. You have the right to challenge a premature MMI determination with your own medical evidence.

faqs.question: How does MMI affect my workers comp benefits in Georgia?
faqs.answer: In Georgia, MMI is when your impairment rating is assigned. It does not by itself end temporary total disability (TTD) — TTD generally continues until you return to work, are released to full duty, or hit the 400-week cap — and permanent partial disability (PPD) (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-263) is paid once TTD or TPD stops. For catastrophic injuries the 400-week caps do not apply (O.C.G.A. §§ 34-9-261, 34-9-200.1). Medical benefits continue after MMI, for up to 400 weeks in non-catastrophic cases.

faqs.question: How does MMI affect my workers comp benefits in South Carolina?
faqs.answer: In South Carolina, MMI lets the insurer ask the Commission to stop TTD (S.C. Code § 42-9-260) and starts the permanent-disability phase — scheduled PPD by impairment rating (§ 42-9-30) or wage-loss benefits (§ 42-9-20). The 500-week overall benefit cap (S.C. Code § 42-9-10) continues to apply. Medical benefits for the work injury can continue after MMI as long as the Commission finds treatment will lessen your disability — but they end one year after a Form 16 settlement is paid out or after a year without authorized treatment, so keep treating (S.C. Code § 42-15-60).

faqs.question: Should I settle my personal injury case before reaching MMI?
faqs.answer: Generally no. Settling before MMI means you do not know the full extent of your injuries or future medical costs. You risk accepting far less than your claim is worth. The exception is catastrophic injuries with obvious permanent disability and low insurance policy limits, where early settlement may make strategic sense.

faqs.question: What can I do if the insurer declares MMI prematurely?
faqs.answer: You can (1) request a second opinion from an independent physician, (2) have your attorney request a hearing — Form WC-14 with Georgia's State Board or Form 50 with South Carolina's Commission, (3) provide additional medical evidence showing you have not yet stabilized, or (4) in Georgia, use your one-time independent examination at the insurer's expense within 120 days of your first income-benefit check (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-202(e)); in South Carolina, ask the Commission to order an examination (S.C. Code § 42-15-80). Do not accept a premature MMI without legal advice.
